```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>")
library(spseg)
library(dplyr)
```

`spseg()` uses Euclidean distance unless a `network` is supplied. In network
mode it measures proximity using shortest paths through a supplied edge list.
Constructing geographic adjacency, preparing road topology, snapping locations,
and allocating population are the user's responsibility. Geometry, if supplied,
is retained for mapping and does not define the network.

## An edge list and population table

```{r supplied-network}
edges <- data.frame(
  from=c("a","b","b","c"),
  to=c("b","c","d","e")
)
nodes <- data.frame(
  node=letters[1:5],
  group_a=c(20,5,0,10,0), group_b=c(0,5,20,0,10),
  low=c(6,2,0,3,0), high=c(0,2,8,0,4)
)
variables <- list(
  ethnicity=spseg_categorical(counts=c("group_a","group_b")),
  income=spseg_continuous(representation = "intervals", counts=c("low","high"))
)
network <- spseg_network(edges)
result <- spseg(nodes, variables, network=network, node_id="node",
                bands=c(1,2), weighting="unweighted", output="full")
as.data.frame(result)
head(as.data.frame(result, what="env"))
```

Every row is an observation attached to exactly one node. Several observations
may occupy the same node, preserving individual values without aggregation.
Nodes present only in the edge list can connect observations without adding
population. Observation nodes absent from the edge list are isolated.
Self-loops and parallel edges do not duplicate population. If an entity is
allocated to several nodes, apportion its counts or weights before calling
spseg; repeating its full population would count that population repeatedly.

The same continuous summary interface works with network neighborhoods. The
two supplied income intervals below preserve the requested median boundary
(`.5`) by proportionally allocating the category that crosses it in global
rank space. The warning and summary metadata report the allocation; this
assumes the same within-category rank distribution at every node. Because the path is undirected here, the example's
outward environments are also reachable in reverse. On a directed network,
rank summaries describe outward reachable neighbors and need not be symmetric.

```{r network-income-summary}
network_income <- spseg(
  nodes,
  variables = list(income = spseg_continuous(
    counts = c("low", "high"),
    representation = "intervals",
    summary = list(type = "quantiles", probs = 0.5, mean_rank = TRUE)
  )),
  network = network,
  node_id = "node",
  bands = c(1, 2),
  weighting = "unweighted",
  measures = "exposure",
  output = "full"
)

as.data.frame(network_income, what = "exposure") |>
  filter(summary == "quantiles") |>
  select(from_group, band, statistic, prob, rank)
network_income$analyses$income$definition$summary[c(
  "requested_probs", "effective_probs", "groups", "interpolation"
)]
```

With `summary = list(type = "shares")`, the default quartile grid still defines
four groups. The two interval categories are apportioned across those groups
at the requested boundaries. Binary continuous pairwise comparisons use those
resolved group shares and the same full-variable network neighborhoods; they
do not rerun shortest paths for each pair.

The categorical, ordinal, grouped continuous and observed continuous variable
specifications and index formulas are the same as for Euclidean environments.
Global reference distributions cover all supplied observations, including those
in other connected components. The interpretation of an environment depends
on the network; using these formulas does not establish every spatial-index
property for an arbitrary directed or weighted graph.

## Costs, direction and kernels

Supply a `cost` column for shortest paths based on summed nonnegative costs.
Costs can express travel time, distance, or another additive measure. Without
costs, each edge has length one and bands are hop counts. Zero costs are allowed.
With `directed=TRUE`, paths follow edges from `from` to `to`, outward from the
focal observation. Reverse the edges to measure incoming proximity.

Traversal costs and kernels have different roles: costs determine distance;
`weighting` then determines contributions within the selected neighborhood.
The default biweight kernel gives zero weight at a radius-band boundary. For
example, with a one-hop band it excludes first-order neighbors through zero
kernel weights. Use `weighting="unweighted"` when all selected hops should
contribute equally. Population KNN also selects its target before applying
the kernel, so its effective weighted population may be smaller.

Network bands must be explicit; there is no implicit conversion from Euclidean
default bands. Network calculations require `surface="raw"` and `search="boost"`.

## Variable-specific population KNN

```{r network-knn}
adaptive <- spseg(nodes, variables, network=network, node_id="node",
                  neighbors="knn", bands=c(10,20), weighting="unweighted")
adaptive$analyses$ethnicity$knn
adaptive$analyses$income$knn
```

One traversal serves the variables. Each selects its own eligible population;
transit nodes add none. The focal observation enters first, fractionally if
necessary. If the remaining population falls within a tied distance group,
every member of that group receives the same inclusion fraction. With $C$
people strictly closer, $B$ in the boundary group, and target $k$, this fraction
is $(k-C)/B$. Weighted paths complete the full distance group, including nodes
reached through zero-cost edges.

An unattainable target raises an error identifying the variable, focal row,
node, and reachable eligible population. A large regional population does not
guarantee that every focal observation can reach the requested population.

## Preparing a small road network with sfnetworks

The following self-contained example places population points on road segments,
inserts network nodes at those positions, and passes the resulting tables to
spseg. No road preparation occurs inside the measurement engine.

```{r road-preparation, eval=requireNamespace("sfnetworks", quietly=TRUE)}
roads <- sf::st_sf(geometry=sf::st_sfc(
  sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(0,0),c(2,0))),
  sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(2,0),c(4,0))), crs=3857
))
population <- sf::st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x=c(.5,3.5), y=0, A=c(30,0), B=c(0,70)),
  coords=c("x","y"), crs=3857
)
roads_network <- sfnetworks::as_sfnetwork(roads, directed=FALSE)
roads_network <- sfnetworks::st_network_blend(roads_network, population)

node_features <- sf::st_as_sf(roads_network, active="nodes")
node_features$node <- seq_len(nrow(node_features))
observations <- node_features[!is.na(node_features$A),]
edge_features <- sf::st_as_sf(roads_network, active="edges")
edge_features$cost <- as.numeric(sf::st_length(edge_features))
edge_table <- sf::st_drop_geometry(edge_features)

prepared <- spseg_network(edge_table, cost="cost", units="metres")
road_result <- spseg(observations,
  list(groups=spseg_categorical(counts=c("A","B"))),
  network=prepared, node_id="node", bands=c(1,3),
  weighting="unweighted", output="full"
)
as.data.frame(road_result)
sf::st_as_sf(road_result, bands=3)
```

These points already lie on their roads. With off-network points, choose an
appropriate snapping tolerance and decide whether access costs should enter
the network. For population known only as a segment total, choose and document
a discrete allocation to nodes or inserted points before measurement.

Geographic polygon adjacency can be prepared similarly: derive pairs using
`sf::st_touches()` or an explicitly chosen shared-boundary rule, attach stable
feature IDs, and supply the resulting edges. spseg does not infer an adjacency
definition from polygon geometry.

## Implementation and attribution

Euclidean queries use Boost.Geometry. Unweighted networks use Boost.Graph
breadth-first traversal; weighted networks use Boost.Graph Dijkstra traversal.
Both are supplied by BH, under the Boost Software License. Graphs use sparse
storage and bounded searches, without a dense all-pairs distance matrix.
Search buffers are reused within a call; graph-only nodes have no population.
The backend is single-threaded and can be called within an external parallel
loop over independent cities or simulations.

- [Boost.Geometry](https://github.com/boostorg/geometry)
- [Boost.Graph](https://github.com/boostorg/graph)
- [BH](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BH)
- [sfnetworks](https://luukvdmeer.github.io/sfnetworks/)
